answer.short:
$$y=\begin{cases}1-2x,&x<0,\\1,&0\le x\le1,\\2x-1,&x>1.\end{cases}$$
The graph has a horizontal segment from $(0,1)$ to $(1,1)$ and upward rays on either side.
answer.worked:
Add the ordinates of $y=|x|$ and $y=|x-1|$. Their vertices divide the graph into three regions.
$$\begin{align*}y&=-x+(1-x)&&\text{for }x<0,\\y&=1-2x;\\y&=x+(1-x)&&\text{for }0\le x\le1,\\y&=1;\\y&=x+(x-1)&&\text{for }x>1,\\y&=2x-1.\end{align*}$$
Join the three pieces at $(0,1)$ and $(1,1)$.

answer.short:
$$y=\begin{cases}-2,&x\le-1,\\2x,&-1\le x\le1,\\2,&x\ge1.\end{cases}$$
The middle segment joins $(-1,-2)$ and $(1,2)$; the outer rays are horizontal.
answer.worked:
Subtract the ordinates of $y=|x-1|$ from those of $y=|x+1|$.
$$\begin{align*}y&=(-x-1)-(1-x)&&\text{for }x\le-1,\\y&=-2;\\y&=(x+1)-(1-x)&&\text{for }-1\le x\le1,\\y&=2x;\\y&=(x+1)-(x-1)&&\text{for }x\ge1,\\y&=2.\end{align*}$$
Join the pieces continuously at $(-1,-2)$ and $(1,2)$.

answer.short:
Domain: $[-3,0)\cup(0,3]$. Vertical asymptote: $x=0$. Closed endpoints: $(-3,\frac13)$ and $(3,-\frac13)$.

The positive branch crosses the $x$-axis at $x=\sqrt{\frac{9-\sqrt{77}}2}$ and $x=\sqrt{\frac{9+\sqrt{77}}2}$. Add the ordinates of the upper semicircle and $y=-\frac{1}{x}$.
answer.worked:
Draw the upper semicircle $y=\sqrt{9-x^2}$ and reflect $y=\frac{1}{x}$ in the $x$-axis. Add their ordinates for $-3\le x\le3$, excluding $x=0$.

On the left, both ordinates are positive, and the graph rises to $+\infty$ as $x\to0^-$. On the right, the graph starts at $-\infty$ as $x\to0^+$, rises above the $x$-axis, then falls to its right endpoint.
$$\begin{align*}y(-3)&=\sqrt{9-9}-\frac1{-3},\\y(-3)&=\frac13;\\y(3)&=\sqrt{9-9}-\frac13,\\y(3)&=-\frac13.\end{align*}$$
For an $x$-intercept, the semicircle ordinate must equal $\frac{1}{x}$, so $x>0$.
$$\begin{align*}\sqrt{9-x^2}&=\frac1x,\\9-x^2&=\frac1{x^2},\\x^4-9x^2+1&=0,\\x^2&=\frac{9\pm\sqrt{77}}2,\\x&=\sqrt{\frac{9\pm\sqrt{77}}2}.\end{align*}$$
Both positive values lie in the domain. The sketch retains both crossings and the exact endpoint heights.

answer.short:
Domain: $-4<x<4$. Vertical asymptotes: $x=-4$ and $x=4$. The graph increases through $(0,0)$ and is symmetric about the origin.

Subtract the two logarithmic ordinates; the graph tends to $-\infty$ at the left asymptote and $+\infty$ at the right asymptote.
answer.worked:
Draw $y=\log_2(x+4)$ and $y=\log_2(4-x)$ lightly, then subtract the second ordinate from the first at each common $x$.
$$\begin{align*}x+4&>0,\\x&>-4;\\4-x&>0,\\x&<4.\end{align*}$$
The common domain is $(-4,4)$. At $x=0$, both logarithmic ordinates are $2$, giving $y=0$. As $x\to-4^+$, the first ordinate tends to $-\infty$ while the second stays finite. As $x\to4^-$, the second ordinate tends to $-\infty$ while the first stays finite, so the difference tends to $+\infty$.

The first component increases and the second decreases, so their difference increases. Replacing $x$ by $-x$ reverses the two terms, giving origin symmetry. Join the ordinate points smoothly between the asymptotes.
